temptingClaims: Doubling the viscosity halves the typical displacement.
whyTempting: The viscosity sits in the denominator of the diffusion coefficient, so doubling it halves \(D\), and that halving seems to carry straight over to the distance a grain travels.
whereItIsTrue: It is true of the diffusion coefficient. § 3 finds \(D = \frac{RT}{N}\frac{1}{6\pi kP}\), with Einstein's \(k\) the viscosity, so doubling \(k\) halves \(D\), and with it the mean square of the displacement at a fixed time.

whatIsTrue.r0: A liquid twice as viscous halves \(D\), but the typical distance goes as the square root of \(D\), so it falls to about 0.71 of its value, not to half.
whatIsTrue.r1: § 5 combines the diffusion coefficient of § 3 with the law \(\lambda_x = \sqrt{2Dt}\) of § 4 to give \(\lambda_x = \sqrt{t}\,\sqrt{\frac{RT}{N}\frac{1}{3\pi kP}}\), and remarks that this equation shows how \(\lambda_x\) must depend on \(T\), \(k\) and \(P\) (p. 559). The viscosity \(k\) sits under the square root. Doubling it halves \(D\) and the mean square \(\lambda_x^2\) at a fixed time, and divides \(\lambda_x\) itself by \(\sqrt{2}\). BM-01's viscosity comparison shows it: at 290.15 K and a radius of 0.5 μm, \(\lambda_x\) after one second is 0.794 μm in a liquid of viscosity \(1.35\times10^{-3}\) Pa·s and 0.561 μm at twice that viscosity, a ratio of 0.707.
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) § 3: \(D = \frac{RT}{N}\frac{1}{6\pi kP}\), where Einstein's \(k\) is the viscosity and \(P\) the radius of a grain. Doubling \(k\) halves \(D\). (2) § 4: \(\lambda_x = \sqrt{2Dt}\), the square root of the mean square of the displacement along one axis. (3) Halve \(D\) at the same \(t\): the mean square \(2Dt\) halves, and its square root is multiplied by \(\sqrt{1/2} = 1/\sqrt{2}\), about 0.707. (4) With the numbers of BM-01's comparison: \(D\) falls from \(3.148\times10^{-13}\) to \(1.574\times10^{-13}\) m²/s, and \(\lambda_x\) at one second from 0.794 μm to 0.561 μm. (5) Halving the distance would take four times the viscosity.
whatIsTrue.r3: Einstein prints the dependence as a formula and gives one worked case, water at 17 °C with \(k = 1{,}35\cdot10^{-2}\) in the units of the time, for which \(\lambda_x\) is 0.8 micron in one second (p. 559). He does not compare two viscosities; the comparison here is made with his law, not taken from his text.

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 17, 549–560 (1905), plates pp. 556 and 559
